title: Unsupervised Learning: Clustering and PCA
text:
Insights

We ran two clustering models to understand what contributes to the popularity of Justin Bieber’s songs: hierarchical and K-means clustering. We began by using the K-means clustering algorithm. We tried the elbow technique; however, the plot was too vague, and it was difficult to determine the best K from such a wide range of values. We then created a silhouette plot to determine the K that maximizes the average silhouette. The silhouette plot was optimal because it clearly indicated that 3 was the best number of clusters, and thus, this means that when we use 3 clusters, the within-cluster variance is small (all the pairs within the clusters are fairly close to one another). However, when we made 3 clusters, as the silhouette plot suggested, we found that the popularity variation across the clusters was minimal. No cluster stood out as most popular (values were all in the 60% range roughly). Next, we tried hand-tuning the algorithm to different numbers of clusters and after trial-and-error (using clusters of 2 up to 8), we found that when we used 4 clusters one of the groups stood out as most popular (77%, vs. the other groups which had 63%, 59%, 58% popularities respectively). Using 4 clusters makes sense because there are no clusters with too few data points, the K is close to the number that the silhouette plot suggested as well as it has one cluster that stands out in regards to popularity.


Looking into cluster 3, which had the highest percentage of popularity, we found several features that stood out within this group. The most popular cluster of Justin Bieber songs had the highest danceability, a higher proportion of songs in the minor key, the lowest instrumentalness, the lowest liveness, and the highest tempo. Cluster 4, the least popular group of songs, had the highest liveness, valence, loudness, and energy measure with a low tempo value. This indicates that although the songs have an upbeat tone, they are slower than the most popular songs. This could contribute to their lack of popularity. Cluster 2 is the third most popular group of songs. This cluster has the lowest valence measure by far, indicating that this group of songs is generally unhappy. Cluster 4 has similar energy to Cluster 3. This means that while the song’s mood is negative or depressing, it maintains high energy levels with a lot of activity or intensity. Cluster 1, the second most popular, is the only cluster with a high acousticness and low energy measure. Additionally, the songs generally are in a lower key and have lower danceability than the rest of Bieber’s songs. Overall, this group of songs is slower, calmer, and acoustic.


Then, we ran a hierarchical model. Our hierarchical model showed a lot of variation within clusters for the heat map which did not allow a lot of opportunities for interpretation. Also, if we had more than 2 clusters, the model would create a cluster with a single song. This once again limited interpretation. Ultimately, we chose to run a K-means clustering model. Overall, K-means allowed for more analysis to understand what traits contributed to Justin Bieber’s most popular songs.

title: Unsupervised Learning: Clustering and PCA
text:
Insights

There is a wide variety of songs – some go viral on TikTok let’s say; hence, they become popular. Others are, although, rich in content and they are not as famous as one could expect. Thus, given the wide variety of predictors and the insights each gives us we applies a ML technique called Principal Component Analysis (PCA). There is a whole bunch of fancy math that goes behind PCA, but just keep in mind that PCA explores patterns in group structures in our columns. While doing this, it is hard to interpret but with the help of your Belieber wizards, we are going to help you disantagle this mysterty of JB’s hits. Let’s explore some graphs to help you understand PCAs.



Given that we want to know how many overall PCAs we should use, we first implement a graph of Cumulative % of variance explained (plot) versus the number of PCs. As you can see, if we only use 1 PC, we can only explain roughly 25% of the variability in JB’s most popular songs – this in nature is our strongest way to go as the variables that are being merged are correlated the most. Nonetheless, we may want to explain a bit more of the variability of the popular songs.




Now, let’s get our hands dirty! This circle plot (called a PCA variable plot) shows how much each musical feature contributes to the first PC (x-axis) and the second PC (y-axis). The main takeaway from this graph is that energy, loudness, and danceability are strongly aligned with PC1. This tells us that PC1 is capturing the “power” or “performance energy” of a song. On the other side, acousticness is pointing in the opposite direction, which means it’s negatively correlated with energy and loudness, the more acoustic a song is, the less energetic and loud it tends to be. PC2 appears to be shaped more by speechiness, duration, and key, which tell us that this component captures songs with longer durations or more spoken lyrical content. To sum all this up, PC1 separates songs by how upbeat and energetic they are, and PC2 adds a layer that reflects structure, vocal delivery, and complexity.




Don’t feel overwhelmed, we know that you want to explore the underlying reasons behind JB’s most popular songs and this requires attention to detail ;). This is our last plot, although PC1 and PC2 explain a good amount of the variability, we might want to consider more PCs, and I would suggest using 4 PCs, because we want to make sure to tackle little details of each song and be careful, but also we want to save you some money and save us the computation expense, we don’t want to overwhelm you, our beloved music manager, so we will use 4PCs, which each shapes the song with their variable as you can see. Note: if the variable bar is above 0 (pointing upwards) it means that it contributes positively and the magnitude of it depends on the height of it, and same if the bar points below 0.



So, you want to know why Justin Bieber is the daddy/king of pop? His most successful hits share 4 characteristics, each using their own style.



High energy and loudness drive popularity: Songs that are high in energy, loud, and very danceable dominate the strongest group (which in my ML analysis I call the first principal component). These songs tend to be the most commercially successful, think of tracks like “Sorry”, “What Do You Mean?”, “Baby,” you name them. Hence, if you are on a low budget and have limited resources, I would suggest you focus on maintaining a strong and energetic vibe, which is key for the audience.




Acoustic and softer songs are less mainstream: On the other side, it is important that you as a manager consider the don’ts! Songs that have higher acousticness (more natural or unplugged feel) tend to move in the opposite direction. While appreciated by loyal fans, these songs are generally less popular in the broader market. Acoustic songs add variety but may not dominate charts unless heavily promoted.




Speechiness and key variety add artistic depth: Some songs with higher speechiness (more spoken lyrics or rhythmic delivery) and interesting changes in musical key form a second group. These often reflect tracks where Justin experiments with new sounds/storytelling formats (aka. “Love Yourself”).




Valence (happiness) matters: Songs with very emotional or sad tones tend to be less popular unless balanced with other upbeat elements like tempo and energy. Even emotional songs need a strong hook or rhythm to maintain mass appeal.

title: H-1B Visa Trends
text:
Most Americans never face the extensive sponsorship requirements necessary to secure employment authorization. As Latinx students from immigrant backgrounds, we’ve witnessed the complex visa application process firsthand, motivating us to investigate: What employment features increase the likelihood of H-1B visa certification?
This dataset originates from the U.S. Department of Labor and was accessed through Kaggle, spanning 2020-2023. Given the dataset’s size, we cleaned the data to focus on H-1B visas for U.S. employment, then drew a stratified random sample of 1% (~33,000 observations) while preserving noisiness. We hypothesize that occupation type, geographical location, application timing, and wage levels will influence certification outcomes.

title: H-1B Visa Trends
text:
Uploading Libraries

# Libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(ggthemes)
library(plotly)
library(leaflet)


Importing the Data

# Uploading the 1%-stratified sample
visas <- read_csv("~/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/hriostorres.gihub.io/data/visas_sample.csv")

# Aggregating our variables of interest
visas <- visas %>%
  mutate(SOC_CODE = str_sub(SOC_CODE, 1, 2)) %>%
  mutate(SOC_TITLE = case_when( #code gotten from stackoverflow
    SOC_CODE == "11" ~ "Management",
    SOC_CODE == "13" ~ "Business and Financial Operations",
    SOC_CODE == "15" ~ "Computer and Mathematical",
    SOC_CODE == "17" ~ "Architecture and Engineering",
    SOC_CODE == "19" ~ "Life, Physical, and Social Science",
    SOC_CODE == "21" ~ "Community and Social Service",
    SOC_CODE == "23" ~ "Legal",
    SOC_CODE == "25" ~ "Educational Instruction and Library",
    SOC_CODE == "27" ~ "Arts, Design, Entertainment, Sports, and Media",
    SOC_CODE == "29" ~ "Healthcare Practitioners and Technical",
    SOC_CODE == "31" ~ "Healthcare Support",
    SOC_CODE == "33" ~ "Protective Service",
    SOC_CODE == "35" ~ "Food Preparation and Serving Related",
    SOC_CODE == "37" ~ "Building and Grounds Cleaning and Maintenance",
    SOC_CODE == "39" ~ "Personal Care and Service",
    SOC_CODE == "41" ~ "Sales and Related",
    SOC_CODE == "43" ~ "Office and Administrative Support",
    SOC_CODE == "45" ~ "Farming, Fishing, and Forestry",
    SOC_CODE == "47" ~ "Construction and Extraction",
    SOC_CODE == "49" ~ "Installation, Maintenance, and Repair",
    SOC_CODE == "51" ~ "Production",
    SOC_CODE == "53" ~ "Transportation and Material Moving",
    SOC_CODE == "55" ~ "Military Specific",
    TRUE ~ "Other"))

grouped_soc_title <-visas %>%
  filter (CASE_STATUS == "Certified") %>% 
  count(SOC_TITLE) %>% 
  arrange(desc(n))

visas <- visas %>% 
  mutate(year = year(RECEIVED_DATE),
         n_week = week(RECEIVED_DATE),
         n_month = month(RECEIVED_DATE)) %>% 
  filter ((year < 2024),
           (EMPLOYER_COUNTRY == "UNITED STATES OF AMERICA"))

title: H-1B Visa Trends
text:
Occupation
We first observe how different occupational categories affect H-1B visa certification outcomes.

# Showing top 10 ocupations arranged by application volume
grouped_soc_title %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%
  slice(1:10) %>% 
  mutate(SOC_TITLE = fct_reorder(SOC_TITLE, n)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = SOC_TITLE)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Occupation by Number of Applications",
    x = "Number of Applications",
    y = "Occupation Category") +
  theme_minimal()




This graph shows how Computer and Mathematical occupations dominate the H1-B application.




Computer and Mathematical occupations dominate H-1B applications with over 20,000 applications—nearly four times more than Architecture and Engineering. This disparity reflects the tech industry’s heavy reliance on H-1B visas for specialized talent.

Case Status Distribution For Visa Applications in Top 10 Occupations

visas_occ <- visas %>% 
  count(SOC_TITLE) %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>% 
  slice(1:10)

p <- visas %>% 
  count(SOC_TITLE, CASE_STATUS) %>%
  semi_join(visas_occ, by = "SOC_TITLE") %>% 
  left_join(visas_occ, by = "SOC_TITLE") %>% 
  group_by(SOC_TITLE) %>%
  mutate(pct = round(n.x / sum(n.x), 3)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
 ggplot(aes(
      x = fct_reorder(SOC_TITLE, n.y),
      y = pct,
      fill = CASE_STATUS,
      text = paste0(
        "Industry: ", SOC_TITLE,
        "<br>Case status: ", CASE_STATUS,
        "<br>Percentage: ", scales::percent(pct, accuracy = 0.1),
        "<br>Applications: ", n.x))) + 
  geom_col() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(y = "Percentage",
       x = "Industries",
       fill = "Case Status",
       title  = "Visa Applications per Occupations (2020-2023)") +
  coord_flip()

ggplotly(p, tooltip = c("text"))



Certification rates by occupation category remain consistently above 90% across all top 10 occupations.


Despite volume differences, certification rates remain consistent across occupations, with most categories exceeding 90%. Life, Physical, and Social Science occupations show slightly higher “Certified-Withdrawn” cases, while denial rates remain minimal across all categories. The lower application volumes in certain categories limit our ability to assess occupation as a predictor of certification.


Decision Timeline By Occupation

# Cleaning Timeline Data

# Converting dates from chr to int
visas$RECEIVED_DATE <- as.Date(visas$RECEIVED_DATE)
visas$DECISION_DATE <- as.Date(visas$DECISION_DATE)

# Calculating timeline in months
visas$VISA_TIMELINE <- as.numeric(visas$DECISION_DATE - visas$RECEIVED_DATE) / 30.44


visas %>% 
  group_by(SOC_TITLE) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_timeline = mean(VISA_TIMELINE, na.rm = TRUE),
    count = n()
  ) %>%
  slice_max(count, n = 10) %>%  # Add this line to get top 10 by count
  arrange(avg_timeline) %>%
  mutate(SOC_TITLE = fct_inorder(SOC_TITLE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_timeline, y = SOC_TITLE, fill = count)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Average Visa Decision Timeline by Occupation",
       x = "Average Timeline (months)",
       y = "Occupations",
       fill = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()




Average visa decision timeline by occupation category. Processing times range from 0.5 months (Community and Social Service) to 2.3 months (Life, Physical, and Social Science).




Processing times vary considerably. Life, Physical, and Social Science applications take over 2 months, while Community and Social Service applications are decided in under one month. Computer and Mathematical occupations experience relatively short processing times despite high volume, suggesting possible prioritization of economically significant industries.

# Setting up the map: Longitude and latitude for each state
states_map <- map_data("state")

# Getting dominant industry per state
dominant_industry <- visas %>%
  group_by(EMPLOYER_STATE, SOC_TITLE) %>%
  summarise(total_applications = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(EMPLOYER_STATE) %>%
  slice_max(total_applications, n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(EMPLOYER_STATE = tolower(state.name[match(EMPLOYER_STATE, state.abb)]))

# Creating a map that shows the dominant industry per state
ggplot(dominant_industry, aes(map_id = EMPLOYER_STATE, fill = SOC_TITLE)) +
  geom_map(map = states_map) +
  expand_limits(x = states_map$long, y = states_map$lat) +
  labs(fill = "Industry", 
    x = "", 
    y = "", 
    title = "Dominant Visa Application Industry by State (2020–2023)") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(drop = TRUE) +
  theme_minimal()




We see that Computer and Mathematical Occupations dominate the H1-B application in most states.




The map above reveals Computer and Mathematical occupations dominate H-1B applications nationwide, particularly in East and West Coast states. These patterns demonstrate that occupation type hugely influences application volume and processing duration. While certification rates appear consistent, the shorter processing times for Computer and Mathematical occupations suggest potential prioritization, likely reflecting both the F-1-to-H-1B pipeline with STEM OPT extensions and tech industry reliance on foreign talent.

title: H-1B Visa Trends
text:
Geographical Location
Our analysis now turns to how geographical location influences H-1B visa certification outcomes and application patterns across different states and regions.

Total Visa Applications per State

# Setting up the map: Longitude and latitude for each state
states_map <- map_data("state")

# Creating a map that shows the number of visas given per state
visas_map <- visas %>% 
  group_by(EMPLOYER_STATE) %>% 
  summarise(number_of_visas = n()) %>% 
  mutate(EMPLOYER_STATE = tolower(state.name[match(EMPLOYER_STATE, state.abb)]))
ggplot(visas_map, aes(map_id = EMPLOYER_STATE, fill = number_of_visas)) +
  geom_map(map = states_map) +
  expand_limits(x = states_map$long, y = states_map$lat) +
  labs(fill = "Number of Applications", x="", y="", title = "Total visa applications per state from 2020 to 2023") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  theme_minimal()




H-1B application volume concentrates heavily in California, Texas, New York, and Washington.




H-1B application volume concentrates heavily in major tech hubs. California accounts for over 5,000 applications, far surpassing other states, with Texas, New York, and Washington also showing high volumes. Most states show minimal application activity, revealing geographic clustering in established technology centers.


Percentage of Certified H1B Applications by State

# Data wrangling for geographical exploration
visas_map <- visas %>% 
  group_by(EMPLOYER_STATE) %>% 
  summarise(
    certified = sum(CASE_STATUS == "Certified", na.rm = TRUE),
    total = n(),
    pct_certified = certified / total
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    EMPLOYER_STATE = tolower(state.name[match(EMPLOYER_STATE, state.abb)])
  )
# Map of certified applications by state 
ggplot(visas_map, aes(map_id = EMPLOYER_STATE, fill = pct_certified)) +
  geom_map(map = states_map) +
  expand_limits(x = states_map$long, y = states_map$lat) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    fill = "% Certified",
    title = "Percentage of Certified H1B Applications by State (2020–2023)",
    x = "", y = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal()




Most states maintain certification rates above 90%, with few exceptions showing rates below 70%.




Certification rates remain relatively high across most states (above 90%), though several states including Nebraska, Oklahoma, and Alabama display notably lower rates (below 70%). These disparities may reflect differences in application quality, industry composition, or sample size effects.

# Data wrangling for visualization
visas_zip <- visas %>% 
  group_by(EMPLOYER_POSTAL_CODE) %>% 
  count(EMPLOYER_POSTAL_CODE) %>% 
  arrange(desc(n)) %>% 
  head(10)

# Create location data with coordinates
location_data <- tibble(
  EMPLOYER_POSTAL_CODE = c("98121", "77845", "94043", "95054", "98052", 
                           "20850", "75082", "19103", "94025", "07094"),
  latitude = c(47.61, 30.5, 37.41, 37.40, 47.68, 
               39.09, 32.99, 39.95, 37.46, 40.78),
  longitude = c(-122.35, -96.3, -122.09, -121.96, -122.12, 
                -77.19, -96.66, -75.17, -122.18, -74.06),
  county = c("King County", "Brazos County", "Santa Clara County", 
             "Santa Clara County", "King County", "Montgomery County",
             "Collin County", "Philadelphia County", "San Mateo County", 
             "Hudson County"),
  city = c("Seattle", "College Station", "Mountain View", "Santa Clara", 
           "Redmond", "Rockville", "Richardson", "Philadelphia", 
           "Menlo Park", "Secaucus"),
  state = c("WA", "TX", "CA", "CA", "WA", "MD", "TX", "PA", "CA", "NJ"),
  country = "USA")

visas_zip_mapped <- visas_zip %>%
  left_join(location_data, by = "EMPLOYER_POSTAL_CODE")

# Color palette for states
pal <- colorFactor(palette = "Set3",
                   levels = unique(visas_zip_mapped$state))

leaflet(data = visas_zip_mapped) %>%
  addTiles() %>%
  addCircleMarkers(
    lng = ~longitude,

Top 10 H-1B visa employer locations in the US


The interactive map reveals the top employer locations: Santa Clara, Mountain View, and Menlo Park—the heart of Silicon Valley—dominate the H-1B market. This concentration aligns with STEM occupations’ dominance in applications.
These patterns demonstrate that while application volume concentrates in tech-dominant states, location has limited influence on certification outcomes overall, with most states maintaining high approval rates. We now shift towards application filing time.

title: H-1B Visa Trends
text:
Time
Next, we look at application timing in H-1B applications to identify whether filing time influences certification outcomes and application volume.

Filing Month Impact on Visa Certification

# Wrangling and plotting case status per month
visas %>% 
  filter(year >= 2020, !is.na(RECEIVED_DATE)) %>% 
  mutate(month_num = month(RECEIVED_DATE),
         month = factor(month.abb[month_num], levels =(month.abb))) %>%
  count(month, CASE_STATUS) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = n, color = CASE_STATUS, group = CASE_STATUS)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    y = "Number of Applications",
    x = "Month in which Application was filed",
    color = "Case Status",
    title = "Case status per filing month (2020–2023)") + 
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_viridis_d()




Application volume peaks in March and October, with certified applications following total volume throughout the year.




Applications show distinct seasonal patterns, with peak filing in March and October. March experiences the highest volume with nearly 3,000 applications, followed by April and May, reflecting the traditional H-1B filing season. October’s secondary peak coincides with the fiscal year start, while July shows the lowest volume due to the annual cap-driven cycle’s completion. So we continue exploring.


Visa Applications Across Years

visas %>% 
  filter(year >= 2020) %>%
  mutate(month = month(RECEIVED_DATE),
          month_name = factor(month(RECEIVED_DATE, label = TRUE), 
                            levels = month.abb)) %>%
  count(month, month_name) %>%
  group_by(month) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = month_name, y = n, fill=month_name)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Monthly Visa Applications across all years") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d("Month") +
  theme_minimal()




March has the highest application volume at nearly 3,000, followed by April and May, with July showing the lowest volume.




To better understand the variation observed in Figure 1, we now visualize total application volume by month across all years in our dataset. March shows the highest volume with nearly 3,000 applications, followed by April and May, reflecting the traditional H-1B filing season. A secondary peak appears in October, coinciding with the start of the fiscal year. July experiences the lowest application volume, likely due to the completion of the annual cap-driven filing cycle.


Visa Certifications Across Months

visas_certified <- visas %>% 
  filter(year >= 2020, !is.na(RECEIVED_DATE)) %>% 
  mutate(month_num = month(RECEIVED_DATE),
         month = factor(month.abb[month_num], levels =(month.abb))) %>%
  count(month, CASE_STATUS) %>% 
  group_by(month) %>% 
  mutate(total_applications = sum(n),
         rate_per_case_status = n/total_applications) %>% 
  filter (CASE_STATUS == "Certified")



 ggplot(visas_certified, aes(x = month, y = rate_per_case_status, group = CASE_STATUS)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    y = "Number of Applications",
    x = "Application filing month",
    color = "Case Status",
    title = "Percentage of Certified Visas for every filing month (2020–2023)") +
  scale_color_viridis_d() + theme_minimal()




Certification rates remain stable throughout the year, ranging between 91-94.5% across all months.




Despite volume differences, certification rates remain remarkably stable throughout the year, ranging between 91-94%. Notable variations include a slight dip to 91% in April during peak season, potentially reflecting rushed petitions, while October shows the highest rate at 94.5%, aligning with renewed processing capacity. November sees an unexpected drop to 90%, possibly due to post-reset backlogs.
The consistency in certification rates across most months, with only minor variations tied to seasonal pressures, suggests timing itself is not a major determinant of approval. Variations appear more closely related to administrative capacity during peak periods rather than systematic bias by month, indicating applicants need not strategically time applications to maximize approval chances.

title: H-1B Visa Trends
text:
Wage
Finally, we examine how wage levels influence H-1B visa certification outcomes, as prevailing wage requirements are a key component of the application process.

Wage Distribution Per Case Status

# Cleaning Wage Data

# Convert all wages to yearly
visas <- visas %>%
  mutate(Yearly_wage = case_when(
    PW_UNIT_OF_PAY == "Hour"  ~ PREVAILING_WAGE * 40 * 52,
    PW_UNIT_OF_PAY == "Week"  ~ PREVAILING_WAGE * 52,
    PW_UNIT_OF_PAY == "Bi-Weekly" ~ PREVAILING_WAGE * 26,
    PW_UNIT_OF_PAY == "Month"  ~ PREVAILING_WAGE * 12,
    PW_UNIT_OF_PAY == "Year"      ~ PREVAILING_WAGE, 
    TRUE ~ NA_real_ ))

# Categorizing wage levels
visas <- visas %>%
  mutate(Wage_Group = factor( if_else(Yearly_wage <56000, "Low", 
                      if_else(Yearly_wage < 170000, "Middle", "High")),
                      levels = c("Low", "Middle", "High"), 
                      ordered = TRUE))


visas %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = CASE_STATUS, y = Yearly_wage)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) format (x, scientific = FALSE)) +
  labs(x = "Case Status", y = "Yearly Wage", title = "Yearly Wage Differentiation Based on Case Status")




Yearly Wage distriution for the different case statuses




Wage distributions across case statuses reveal interesting patterns. Certified applications show a wider wage range ($17,420-$400,000) compared to denied applications ($17,576-$239,200), reflecting that approved positions typically require specialized skills commanding higher pay.
Certified-withdrawn applications average $88,712 yearly, slightly lower than fully withdrawn applications at $93,558. This suggests applicants with higher-wage positions might strategically withdraw before potential denial to maintain cleaner records for reapplication, while certified-withdrawn cases represent routine administrative corrections.


Average Wage for the 10 Industries with the Highest Number of Certified Cases

TOP_10 <- visas %>%
  group_by(SOC_TITLE) %>%
  summarise(total_apps = n(),
    certified_count = sum(CASE_STATUS == "Certified", na.rm = TRUE),
    prcnt_cert = 100 * mean(CASE_STATUS == "Certified", na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_wage = mean(Yearly_wage, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  arrange(desc(certified_count)) %>%
  slice(1:10) %>%
  ungroup()

ggplot(TOP_10, aes(x = avg_wage, y = reorder(SOC_TITLE, avg_wage), fill=prcnt_cert)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Average Wages for 10 Industries with Highest Percentage of Cetified Cases",
    x = "Average Yearly Wage",
    y = "Occupation") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  theme_minimal() 




Overage wage for the 10 industries who have the highest percentage of certified applications




Examining the top 10 industries by certification percentage reveals no clear relationship between average wages and certification rates. Management occupations show the highest average wage around $150,000 with high certification rates, while Computer and Mathematical occupations average $105,000 despite having among the highest certification percentages. Life, Physical, and Social Science occupations show relatively lower wages but maintain strong certification rates.
These findings suggest wage level alone doesn’t determine approval likelihood. The lack of a clear wage-certification pattern across industries, combined with geographical wage disparities, indicates that meeting prevailing wage requirements for specific positions and locations matters more than absolute wage amounts. Combined with earlier findings, occupation type emerges as the most influential factor, with wage playing a supporting role.

title: H-1B Visa Trends
text:
Conclusion
Our analysis reveals that occupation type is the primary factor influencing H-1B visa outcomes, while geographical location, application timing, and wage levels play minimal roles in certification decisions. Computer and Mathematical occupations dominate applications and receive shorter processing times, supporting our hypothesis that occupation determines outcomes. Certification rates remain consistently high (90%+) across most states, months, and wage levels.

Key takeaways: Tech industry reliance on H-1B visas creates concentrated application volumes in Silicon Valley and major tech hubs. While seasonal filing patterns exist, timing doesn’t affect approval likelihood. Wage levels matter only insofar as they meet prevailing wage requirements for specific positions.
Limitations: With more time, we would analyze employer-specific patterns, examine cap-subject versus cap-exempt petitions, and investigate denial reasons more deeply to provide applicants with more actionable insights for improving certification chances. Access to applicant demographic data, such as birthplace, age, education, would also allow for a richer study of disparities in certification outcomes.

title: Wage Disparities Research
Wage Disparities Research
text:
Results?

Females earn approximately 32.7% less than males, primarily due to intangible factors such as employer bias and statistical discrimination.
The analysis further reveals that non-citizen women face an additional 7.9% wage penalty beyond the independent effects of gender and citizenship alone.
Additionally, Naturalized citizens earn about 3.7% more than native-born citizens, likely due to positive selection and legal protections.

I created a multilingual website—built using Quarto and hosted on GitHub Pages—to support voters as they navigate the upcoming Bolivia 2025 national elections.
The site features:

In-depth candidate profiles
Summarized and official party platforms

Interactive decision-support tools
Availability in Spanish, Quechua, Aymara, Guaraní, English, and more — because democracy should speak everyone’s language.

title: 2025 Bolivia Elections Website
text:
Author’s Note
With Bolivia facing an economic crisis, a growing parallel exchange rate, and deep political polarization across departments, the August 17th elections are more than a vote—they’re a turning point.
This project aims to inform, clarify, and empower. There’s a lot of speculation about each candidate’s platform. To help cut through the noise, I gathered and organized reliable, verifiable information into one publicly available platform.
Each profile includes a summary of the candidate’s platform, as well as a link to their official government plan filed with the Tribunal Supremo Electoral.

This is a personal, nonpartisan project driven by the hope for a more informed, inclusive, and democratic Bolivia.
